[[File:Dr. Rikitaro Fujisawa LCCN2014714935.jpg|thumb|upright|Fujisawa in 1922]]
'''Rikitarō Fujisawa''' (Japanese: 藤沢 利喜太郎, ''Fujisawa Rikitarō''; 12 October 1861 – 23 December 1933) was a Japanese mathematician. During the [[Meiji era]] he was instrumental in reforming mathematics education in Japan and establishing the ideas of European mathematics in Japan.

==Biography==
Born in [[Sado Province]] as the eldest son of Oyano Fujisawa, vassal of the shōgun, Rikitarō Fujisawa graduated in 1882 from the Faculty of Sciences of the University of Tokyo. From 1883 to 1887 he studied mathematics in Europe. After study at the [[University of London]] and the [[Humboldt University of Berlin]], he studied at the [[University of Strasbourg]] (then a part of Germany) and in 1886<ref>{{cite book|editor=Gaul, Wolfgang|editor2=Pfeifer, Dietmar|title=From Data to Knowledge|year=2013|page=124|isbn=9783642799990|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=o0DtCAAAQBAJ&pg=PA124}}</ref> attained his doctorate with a dissertation on partial differential equations under the direction of [[Elwin Christoffel]]. In 1887 Fujisawa was appointed the second titular professor of mathematics at the University of Tokyo.<ref>{{cite book|title=The intersection of history and mathematics|author=Sasaki, Chikara|author2=Sigiura, Mitsuo|author3=Dauben, Joseph Warren|authorlink3=Joseph Dauben|year=2013|pages=183|isbn=9783034875219|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=pm0FCAAAQBAJ&pg=PA183}} The first titular professor of mathematics at the U. of Tokyo was [[Kikuchi Dairoku]].</ref>

{{quotation|He was Japan's delegate to the [[International Congress of Mathematicians#History|Second International Conference on Mathematics, Paris, 1900]], and also to the International Commission on the Teaching of Mathematics, 1910. Although a mathematician by training, Dr. Fujisawa has written many articles on international politics.<ref>{{cite book|editor=Kawakami, Kiyoshi Karl|chapter=Chapter II. ''The Monroe Doctrine and the League of Nations'' by Professor Rikitaro Fujisawa|title=What Japan Thinks|publisher=Macmillan|year=1921|pages=[https://archive.org/details/cu31924023233327/page/n24 21]–48|url=https://archive.org/details/cu31924023233327}}</ref>}}

Fujisawa, who himself attended the seminary of [[Theodor Reye]] in Strasbourg, introduced the institution of the research seminary based on the German model early on.<ref>{{cite journal|author = Kümmerle, Harald|title = Fujisawa Rikitarō to kenkyū gimu|journal=Arīna|issue = 21|year = 2018|pages=97–105|url=https://www.academia.edu/37943456}}</ref> He was a teacher and mentor of several Japanese mathematicians who gained international reputations. His most famous student was [[Teiji Takagi]].<ref>{{cite book|author=Ikeo, Aiko|title=A History of Economic Science in Japan|year=2014|page=97|isbn=9781317747536|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4rJEAwAAQBAJ&pg=PA97}}</ref> In 1921, Fujisawa retired from the University of Tokyo and, beginning in 1925, was twice appointed to the [[House of Peers (Japan)|Japanese House of Peers]] but died in the early part of his second term.

Two of his sons achieved prominence in Japanese society. One of his brothers, Iwao Fujisawa, was a [[rear admiral]] in the Imperial Japanese Navy.
